scenario.name: AI tutor
scenario.idea: A homework tutor for high school students that stores each student's answers and progress.

advisor.summary: This homework tutor stores minors' answers, progress and chat logs and sends them to a third-party AI model, so the biggest risks are student-data privacy, data sharing with the API vendor, and unsafe or wrong AI output for minors. Because only North Carolina users are listed, the pointers below are limited to NC and general US sources, and several risks depend on facts you haven't given (school contracts, student ages, vendor terms).

risks.severityWhy: Meets the 'minors' data' criterion: stores identifiable records and chat logs of high school students with no safeguards described.
risks.title: Collecting and keeping more minor data than needed
risks.why: Chat logs and progress records can reveal grades, struggles, personal disclosures and family details. Over-collection, indefinite retention, or using the data for purposes you did not tell users about may be treated as an unfair or deceptive data practice.
risks.fix: List each data field and its purpose, and drop what the tutor doesn't need. Set a retention limit with automatic deletion of chat logs. Give students and parents a way to view and delete their data. Keep student data out of marketing and model training. Keep your privacy notice consistent with these practices.

risks.severityWhy: Meets the 'minors' data' criterion: student records may fall under child- or education-specific privacy rules, and no consent or school-contract approach is described.
risks.title: Child and student privacy laws may apply (not covered by the source list)
risks.why: Products that serve minors, and products used through schools, may be subject to federal or state child and student privacy rules, including parental consent and school-contract requirements. None of the listed sources directly addresses this, so it needs professional review.
risks.fix: Decide whether you will sell direct to families or through schools. Build an age gate and a parental consent or school-authorization flow to match. Keep a data map showing who can access student records.

risks.severityWhy: Meets the 'minors' data' criterion: student chat logs are sent to a third-party API with no safeguards described.
risks.title: Student data leaking through the third-party AI API
risks.why: Chat logs may contain names, schools and personal details that go to an outside vendor. The vendor may retain or train on them, and prompt injection could expose other students' stored data to the model.
risks.fix: Strip names and identifiers before calling the API. Send only the current session's context, never other students' records. Sign vendor terms for zero retention and no training on your data. Use the model without access to your database, and apply per-student access controls on your side.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: you hold personal information about NC users, so you need a breach plan before scaling.
risks.title: No breach response plan for stored student records
risks.why: Stored answers, progress data and chat logs are a target. If a breach exposes NC residents' personal information, NC's breach notification rules may apply.
risks.fix: Encrypt data at rest and in transit. Use role-based access with audit logs. Write an incident response runbook that names who decides on notification. Keep an inventory of what personal data you hold so you can scope a breach quickly.

risks.severityWhy: Meets the 'direct harm to people' criterion: minors could receive wrong, inappropriate or harmful AI output, and no safeguard is described.
risks.title: Made-up answers and inappropriate content for minors
risks.why: Generative models can give confident wrong answers, produce unsuitable content, or respond poorly if a student discloses distress. Wrong answers also undermine the product's educational purpose.
risks.fix: Add a system prompt and an output filter tuned for teens. Add a crisis-keyword path that shows human help resources instead of a model reply. Ground math and science answers in checked solutions where possible. Add a 'report a bad answer' button and review flagged chats.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: progress data informs a human (teacher or parent), and skewed assessments could affect students before wider release.
risks.title: Skewed progress assessments shaping how humans view students
risks.why: If the AI scores or summarizes student ability, it may do worse for English learners, students with disabilities, or different writing styles. A teacher or parent may over-trust those summaries.
risks.fix: Test the tutor's feedback and progress summaries across student groups and language backgrounds. Label summaries as AI estimates, not grades. Show the evidence behind each summary. Let the human reviewer and the student contest or correct it. Document who sees the data and how it may be used. Ban use for discipline or placement without separate review.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: AI tutoring claims and undisclosed bot interactions with minors need mitigation before wider release.
risks.title: Misleading claims or undisclosed AI in marketing and the product
risks.why: Claims such as 'improves grades' or 'always correct', or students and parents not knowing they are talking to an AI, may raise deceptive-practice concerns.
risks.fix: Label the tutor as AI in the interface and in onboarding. Only make outcome claims you can back with evidence. Be specific in the privacy notice about what is stored and shared with the AI vendor.

risks.severityWhy: Good practice: pending NC bills may affect chatbots or privacy but their scope is unknown.
risks.title: Pending NC chatbot and privacy legislation
risks.why: NC bills on AI chatbots or privacy, especially those involving minors, may change your obligations.
risks.fix: Assign someone to check the NC General Assembly site on a regular schedule. Keep consent, retention and AI-disclosure settings configurable so you can adapt quickly.

askLawyer: Which federal and NC child and student privacy rules apply to us, and does selling through schools versus directly to families change what consent and contracts we need?
What should our contract with the third-party AI vendor say about retention, training on student data, and breach notification?
Are our planned AI disclosures and marketing claims about learning outcomes low-risk under NC deceptive-practice rules?

plain.text:
# Risk Assessment: High School AI Homework Tutor (North Carolina)

## Highest-priority risks

### 1. Student privacy and legal compliance
- **FERPA:** If schools or districts provide the product or student records, you're likely a "school official" handling education records. That requires a contract limiting data use, and the school keeps control of the data.
- **COPPA:** High schoolers are mostly 13+, but 9th graders, early-college students, and accelerated students may be under 13. Without age gating, you risk collecting data from children without verifiable parental consent.
- **North Carolina law:** NC has a student online privacy statute for school-service providers (G.S. 115C-401.2) that limits targeted advertising, profiling, and selling student data. NC also has breach notification requirements (G.S. 75-65). Verify current requirements with counsel.
- **Other:** PPRA if you collect surveys or sensitive info, and CIPA-related district requirements. Many districts also require their own data privacy agreements.
- **Risk:** Sales to districts stall, contracts are breached, or you face FTC or state AG enforcement.

### 2. Sensitive data in chat logs
Students will disclose more than homework: mental health struggles, abuse, sexuality, immigration status, family problems, and self-harm. Chat logs are far more sensitive than answer data.
- **Self-harm and crisis:** The model might respond badly, or no one sees the disclosure in time.
- **Mandatory reporting:** NC has broad child-abuse reporting duties (G.S. 7B-301). You need a clear policy on what the system and your staff do when a disclosure appears, and who is responsible.
- **Secondary use:** Retaining logs indefinitely, using them for training, or sharing them creates long-term harm and liability.

### 3. Third-party API exposure
- Student data flows to a vendor you don't control. Check retention, training-on-data defaults, subprocessors, data location, and breach notification terms.
- The API provider's terms may restrict use with minors or require specific safeguards.
- Vendor model changes, deprecations, outages, or price hikes can disrupt a school-year product.
- You'll need a zero-data-retention or equivalent agreement, and your school contracts must accurately describe this data flow.

### 4. Child safety and content
- Inappropriate, sexual, violent, or biased outputs, and jailbreaks by creative teenagers.
- Emotional dependence on a chatbot, or students treating it as a confidant.
- Inappropriate relationships or manipulation, including users impersonating tutors or peers if there's any social feature.
- Harmful advice on health, safety, or college and legal decisions.

## Educational and product risks

### 5. Accuracy and learning quality
- Hallucinated or incorrect answers, especially in math, science, and history, delivered confidently. Students often can't tell.
- Giving answers instead of teaching, which undermines learning and encourages dependence.
- Misalignment with NC Standard Course of Study, teacher methods, or EOC/AP expectations.
- Academic integrity: teachers may see the tool as a cheating enabler, and students may be accused of misconduct.

### 6. "Informs a human" decisions
Even if humans make the final call, progress reports can shape how teachers, parents, or counselors see a student.
- **Automation bias:** Staff over-trust AI-generated summaries or risk scores.
- **Labeling:** A student flagged as "struggling" or "at risk" may be treated differently, with self-fulfilling effects.
- **Bias:** Performance may differ for English learners, students with disabilities, dialect speakers, and students with limited technology access, so analytics may misread these groups.
- **Transparency:** Students and parents may not know what is recorded, who sees it, or how to contest it.

## Operational and security risks

### 7. Security
- A centralized store of minors' academic records and chat logs is a prime target.
- Risks include account takeover, weak authentication for students, over-broad staff access, insecure logging, and prompt injection that exposes other students' data.
- Schools are frequent ransomware targets, and your product extends the attack surface.

### 8. Access and governance
- Who can see a student's chats: parents, teachers, admins, or your staff?
- Students turning 18 gain their own rights over their records.
- Deletion and retention: end of year, transfer, or contract termination.
- Parents may demand access, while students may expect confidentiality.

### 9. Equity and access
- Uneven home internet and device access, with the risk of widening gaps.
- Accessibility needs (screen readers, IEP/504 accommodations).
- Rural and under-resourced NC districts may be less equipped to evaluate vendors, which raises your responsibility.

### 10. Business and reputational
- A single incident involving a minor (a harmful response or a leak) can end district relationships.
- Media and parent backlash over "AI surveilling kids."
- Changing state and federal AI-in-education rules. NC DPI has issued AI guidance for schools, so check current versions.

## Recommended mitigations

| Area | Actions |
|---|---|
| **Data** | Collect only what's needed. Set short retention windows. Don't train on student data. Support deletion and export. Separate identity from chat content where possible. |
| **Vendor** | Zero-retention terms, a signed DPA, subprocessor transparency, and a fallback model or provider. |
| **Safety** | Content filters, a tuned system prompt, red-teaming with teen-style misuse, crisis detection with escalation to humans, and clear on-screen crisis resources. |
| **Pedagogy** | Socratic or hint-first design, citations or worked steps, subject-matter review of outputs, and teacher controls. |
| **Human oversight** | Present AI summaries as suggestions with their basis. Train staff on limitations. Avoid risk scores or labels without explanation and a way to dispute them. |
| **Governance** | Role-based access, an audit log, a written policy for parent, teacher, and student visibility, and age gating. |
| **Security** | SSO via the school, MFA for staff, encryption, penetration testing, and an incident response plan with NC breach notification timelines. |
| **Transparency** | Plain-language notices for students and parents, and a clear AI disclosure. |
| **Legal** | Counsel review of FERPA, COPPA, and NC law. Prepare district-ready privacy documentation. |
| **Evaluation** | Test accuracy and learning outcomes across student subgroups before and after launch. |

## Key questions to resolve early
1. Is it sold to districts (FERPA path) or directly to families (COPPA and consumer path)?
2. Who sees chat logs, and what happens when a student discloses harm?
3. What does your API vendor retain, and can you contractually prevent training use?
4. What exactly will teachers or parents be told, and could that cause harm to a student?

I can go deeper on any of these, such as a crisis-escalation design or a district-ready privacy checklist.
